title: Zelenskyy Rebuts Trump: Russia Still Hits Ukrainian Energy Sites Amid Alleged Ceasefire Claim
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told an audience at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday that Russia’s air raids on Ukraine’s power grid continue unabated, contradicting recent statements by U.S. President Donald Trump that a de‑facto “energy cease‑fire” was in place. While Kyiv is prepared to suspend its own strikes on Russian energy sites, the Kremlin has not reciprocated, leaving millions of Ukrainians without reliable electricity as winter approaches.

Zelenskyy’s remarks came after President Trump, during a press briefing in Washington, suggested that both sides were “showing restraint” in targeting energy infrastructure, implying an informal truce that had not been formally negotiated. The Ukrainian leader stressed that any such cease‑fire must be mutual and verifiable, noting that Russian missiles have repeatedly hit substations, thermal plants and fuel depots across the country since the start of the year. “We are ready to stop attacks on Russian energy facilities, but Russia must stop attacking ours,” Zelenskyy said, adding that the continued assaults are “a war crime against civilians.”

The discrepancy between the two presidents’ narratives underscores the growing divergence in U.S. policy toward the conflict. Since taking office, Trump has signaled a desire to reduce American involvement, often downplaying the intensity of Russian aggression. Critics argue that his comments risk normalising Russia’s tactics, which have increasingly targeted civilian infrastructure to undermine morale and force political concessions. Ukrainian officials, Western allies, and energy experts warn that sustained attacks on the grid could trigger a humanitarian crisis, especially as temperatures drop and heating becomes a matter of life and death.

Analysts note that Russia’s strategy of striking energy facilities is part of a broader campaign to erode Ukraine’s resilience. By disrupting power supplies, Moscow hopes to cripple industrial output, hamper military communications and sow public discontent. The attacks have already forced large swathes of the country into rolling blackouts, prompting emergency measures such as the deployment of mobile generators and the acceleration of repairs by Ukrainian energy firms. International donors have responded with aid packages that include generators, fuel, and technical assistance, but the scale of the damage outpaces these efforts.

The diplomatic fallout from Trump’s assertion may also affect ongoing negotiations in Brussels and Kyiv’s access to Western military aid. NATO allies have repeatedly called for a clear, enforceable cease‑fire on energy targets, arguing that protecting civilian infrastructure is a prerequisite for any credible peace talks. Ukraine’s willingness to reciprocate, as Zelenskyy emphasized, could serve as a confidence‑building measure, but only if Moscow demonstrates a comparable commitment. So far, Russian officials have dismissed the notion of a cease‑fire, framing the strikes as “legitimate military operations” aimed at disabling Ukraine’s war‑making capacity.

Looking ahead, the situation remains precarious. With winter looming, the international community faces mounting pressure to deliver additional power‑generation assets and to press Moscow into a verifiable halt to its energy attacks. Kyiv has signalled that any future negotiations will hinge on the cessation of strikes against its grid, while the United States appears divided over how forcefully to confront the Kremlin’s tactics. The coming weeks will likely determine whether the rhetoric of an “energy cease‑fire” can be translated into concrete action, or whether Ukraine’s power infrastructure will continue to bear the brunt of a war that shows no sign of abating.
